questions.question: Describe a promise's states and the timing of its executor and handlers. What happens if resolve is called twice?
questions.answer:
A promise is pending, then settles exactly once as fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason. Once settled it is immutable: later resolve or reject calls are ignored, and the first settlement wins. The executor passed to new Promise runs synchronously, immediately, before the constructor returns. The handlers registered with then, catch, and finally always run asynchronously in a microtask, even when the promise is already fulfilled.

That timing explains the classic output order: executor code first, then synchronous code after the promise creation, then handlers. If the executor throws, the promise rejects automatically. A promise that never calls resolve or reject stays pending forever, which is how a hung request leaks memory and never runs its finally cleanup.
key_points: States: pending, fulfilled, rejected
Settles once; later resolve/reject calls are ignored
Executor runs synchronously; handlers run in microtasks
A never-settled promise stays pending forever

questions.question: Compare Promise.all, allSettled, race and any. Give one use case for each.
questions.answer:
Promise.all waits for every input and fulfils with an array in input order, but rejects immediately if any input rejects (fail-fast). Use it when every result is required, such as loading the user, their permissions, and their settings before rendering a page.

Promise.allSettled also waits for every input but never rejects for individual failures; it returns { status, value } or { status, reason } per item. Use it for batch uploads or reports where partial success is useful. Promise.race settles with the first input to settle, fulfilment or rejection, and ignores the rest. Use it for timeouts by racing a request against a timer. Promise.any fulfils with the first success and ignores rejections; if all reject it throws an AggregateError. Use it for redundant mirrors where the fastest healthy response is enough.
key_points: all: all must succeed, input order, fail-fast
allSettled: always fulfils, per-item status
race: first settled wins, including rejection
any: first fulfilled wins; all fail → AggregateError

questions.answer:
It prints after forEach, item 1, item 2, item 3, got: undefined.

The first handler does not return anything: n + 1 is evaluated and discarded, so the next then receives undefined. Use return n + 1 to pass 2 along. The second then is therefore not ready immediately; it waits for the first handler's promise to settle, which takes extra microtask ticks.

forEach is synchronous: it starts each async callback and returns without waiting. The callbacks pause at await Promise.resolve() and resume in microtasks, printing the items. console.log("after forEach") is synchronous, so it runs before all pending microtasks. forEach also discards the promises, so you cannot await completion — use for...of with await or Promise.all(items.map(...)).
key_points: No return in a then handler → next step gets undefined
Handlers always run asynchronously
forEach does not await async callbacks
Use for...of or Promise.all for async iteration

questions.answer:
Output order:
all: bad
race: fast
settled: [ 'fulfilled', 'rejected' ]
any: ok

Promise.all rejects as soon as any input rejects, so its catch is queued first and does not wait for the 20 ms timer. Promise.race also settles on the first rejection, which is immediate, so race prints next. The 5 ms timers then fire: allSettled reports one fulfilled and one rejected, and any ignores the rejection and resolves with the first success, ok.

The lesson: all is all-or-nothing and fail-fast; allSettled collects every outcome; race cares about the first settlement, including failure; any cares only about the first success. Choosing the wrong one is how dashboards go blank because one optional widget failed.
key_points: all rejects immediately on the first failure
race settles on first fulfilment or rejection
allSettled waits and reports every status
any ignores rejections until all fail

questions.answer:
It prints 2, then [ 3, Promise { 4 } ], then first.

Returning a promise from a then handler flattens it: the awaited chain resolves to 2, not to a promise. The third chain returns an array containing a promise. Arrays are not thenables, so the chain does not flatten their contents or wait for them; the awaited value is the array as-is, with a fulfilled promise inside.

A promise settles once: resolve("first") wins and the later reject is ignored, so p logs first with no catch. If you need the values inside an array of promises, return Promise.all([v, Promise.resolve(4)]). This is the difference between adopting a thenable and merely putting a promise inside a container.
key_points: Returning a promise flattens one level
Arrays are not thenables and are not flattened
First settlement wins; later resolve/reject calls are ignored
Use Promise.all to resolve promises inside an array
